Name: Eight Thousand Slave Soldiers Take the Oath: the Legion That Earned Its Freedom
RagShortTexts: After the disaster at Cannae, the Roman Senate broke a class taboo and paid to buy eight thousand young slaves
They formed a volunteer slave legion led by Gracchus, promised freedom in exchange for deeds in battle
At the great victory of Beneventum the slave soldiers fought with no thought for their lives and finally won citizenship and the cap of freedom
BaseText: The Battle of Cannae cost nearly seventy thousand young men, and Rome's citizens of military age were almost all dead or wounded, so the Senate had to break the sacred iron rule, centuries old, that only free citizens could serve in the army. The Senate used public funds to buy eight thousand strong young slaves from the great families and formed them into the 'volunteers' (Volones), led by the plebeian consul Tiberius Gracchus. Gracchus swore a sacred oath to them: whoever took an enemy's head on the battlefield would be freed on the spot. At the Battle of Beneventum in 214 BC, the slave soldiers fought for their lives against the fierce Carthaginian troops and in the end won a great victory. Before the whole army, Gracchus placed on the heads of the slaves who had earned it the brimless Phrygian cap (Pileus) that symbolized freedom, forging these slaves into the Republic's most steadfast iron-blooded guard.

Variants.Content: Rome's greatness lies not in never suffering disaster, but in this: even its slaves, under the banner of the Republic, can burst forth in fighting spirit for freedom with a courage that astonishes the gods!
Yesterday we were beasts of burden under the whip; today the consul gives us short swords and shields. To wash away our slavery and become free men, we will gladly shed every drop of our blood!
The Romans actually make lowly slaves put on heavy armor and go to war. Their proud citizen legions exist only in name; they are clinging to life by relying on slaves.
